title: But Now They Mock Me: Job's Present Humiliation
summary: Job contrasts his former honor with his present disgrace. The sons of outcasts, men he once would not have trusted with his sheepdogs, now mock him, spit at him, and attack him like soldiers breaching a wall. His body is wracked with pain and fever, and God has thrown him into the mud. He cries out to God, who does not answer, and he mourns that though he wept for others in trouble, no one helps him.
story: This is the second part of Job's final monologue (chapters 29 to 31). In chapter 29 he recalled the months gone by, when God watched over him and the whole city honored him. The word now, which opens this chapter and returns in verses 9 and 16, marks the painful reversal. Chapter 29 ended with Job sitting like a king among his troops; chapter 30 begins with him mocked by the lowest members of society. The chapter moves from human contempt (verses 1-15) to God's hostility (verses 16-23) to Job's final lament (verses 24-31). It prepares for chapter 31, where Job will take a formal oath of innocence and demand that God answer.
historical:
The chapter describes the lowest class of ancient Near Eastern society: people who had been driven out of their communities and lived in the wilderness, scavenging for food among desert shrubs, sheltering in holes and caves in the sides of dry riverbeds (wadis). Such outcasts existed on the margins of every settled society, and their lives were extremely precarious. Job describes them with the contempt of a man who once stood at the top of the social order, and he says their fathers were not fit to be trusted with his sheepdogs (verse 1). Dogs in the ancient Near East were mostly scavengers and working animals, not pets, so this is a sharp insult.

The military imagery of verses 12-14, laying snares, building siege ramps, and pouring through a wide breach, reflects the siege warfare of the ancient world. Attackers built earthen ramps against city walls and poured in once the wall was breached. Job pictures himself as a city under assault by the rabble.
cultural:
Spitting in someone's face (verse 10) was among the gravest insults in the ancient world, a sign of utter contempt (compare Numbers 12:14 and Deuteronomy 25:9). Becoming a byword (verse 9) meant being turned into a proverb, a name used as an example of disaster. The plants of verses 4 and 7, mallow (a salty plant that grows in dry and salty ground), the broom tree, and nettles, are the vegetation of the desert fringe; eating them was a sign of desperate hunger. The broom tree is the shrub under which Elijah lay down in despair (1 Kings 19:4).

Job's description of his body in verses 17 and 30 matches the disease described in the prologue (2:7-8): pain that gnaws at night, skin that blackens and peels, and burning fever. The jackals and ostriches of verse 29 were desert creatures known for their mournful cries (Micah 1:8 pairs them in the same way), and to be their brother and companion was to share their lonely lament. The harp and flute of verse 31, instruments once used for joy, now play only mourning, a reversal of the celebrations of the wicked Job described in 21:12.
literary: The chapter is a lament, built on the contrast with chapter 29. Its three sections are each introduced by the word now (verses 1, 9, and 16). In the first section Job describes the social outcasts who now mock him (verses 1-8). In the second he describes their attacks (verses 9-15), using images of war and storm. In the third he turns to God (verses 16-23), addressing him directly as You and accusing him of cruelty: You do not answer, You have ruthlessly turned on me. The final verses (24-31) return to Job's inner state, closing with images of darkness, mourning, and music turned to weeping. Several points in the chapter echo chapter 29 exactly. Where Job was once a father to the needy (29:16), he now asks whether he did not grieve for the needy (30:25); where he once walked through darkness by God's light (29:3), he now looks for light and darkness falls (30:26).

outline.t: Mocked by the sons of outcasts
Their attacks and the loss of Job's dignity
God has thrown me into the mud

doctrines.note: The chapter shows suffering in its full range: physical pain, social humiliation, and the feeling of being abandoned and even attacked by God. Scripture does not minimize any of these. Job's lament is included in the Bible as a truthful account of what suffering can feel like.

Job cries out to God and says that God does not answer (verse 20). This is itself a prayer: Job speaks to God directly even when accusing him. Like the lament psalms, the chapter shows that complaint addressed to God is a form of faith.

Job's contempt for the outcasts in verses 1-8 is uncomfortable to read. He who defended the poor still looks down on those at the very bottom. The chapter shows even a righteous man's limits, and it sets up the Bible's larger teaching that all people share the same maker (a point Job himself makes in 31:15).

words.note: Attah, now. It appears three times in this chapter (verses 1, 9, and 16) and marks each stage of Job's descent. The repeated word draws a line between the past of chapter 29 and the present reality.

Oni, affliction or misery. It describes the state of being humbled, oppressed, or brought low. Job speaks of days of affliction in verses 16 and 27. The word is related to ani, the afflicted or poor, whom Job once protected and among whom he now finds himself.

Yeshuah, salvation, deliverance, or welfare. In verse 15 the BSB translates it as prosperity: Job's well-being has passed away like a cloud. The same word appears in 13:16, where Job hoped that his coming before God would be his salvation.
Tan, jackal. Jackals roamed ruins and deserted places and were known for their howling at night. In verse 29 Job calls himself a brother of jackals, an image of loneliness and mourning.

christ: Several details of this chapter find thematic echoes in the Gospels' account of the passion of Jesus. Job is mocked in song and made a byword, spat upon, and attacked by those who once would have honored him. The Gospels describe Jesus mocked by soldiers and passers-by, spat upon (Mark 14:65; 15:19), and abandoned by those who had followed him. Job cries out to God and receives no answer (verse 20); Jesus cried out on the cross, asking why God had forsaken him (Mark 15:34). The difference is also important. Job's suffering was not chosen, and he protests it; Jesus went to the cross willingly, and the New Testament says he bore the sins of others. The link is not prediction but pattern: the righteous sufferer mocked and abandoned. It helps explain why the early church found in Job and in the lament psalms a language for the suffering of Christ.

hard.q: How can Job, who defended the poor, speak with such contempt about the outcasts in verses 1-8?
hard.a: Many readers are troubled by this section. Job describes the men who mock him as a senseless and nameless brood, driven out of the land, whose fathers were not fit to be trusted with his dogs. It seems inconsistent with the Job of chapter 29, who was a father to the needy. Some interpreters say this reveals a real flaw in Job: his charity flowed downward from a position of honor, and he never regarded the very lowest as his equals. The later chapters of the book, in which God humbles Job, may address this. Others read the section as the bitterness of a man in extreme pain, not as his settled view. His point is not to despise the poor but to show how far he has fallen, that even the lowest now look down on him. A third reading notes that these are not simply the poor but people who have joined in cruelty against a suffering man. The text supports elements of all three. What is clear is that even a righteous man's words in suffering are not all to be imitated, and the book lets us see Job whole.

questions: Job's suffering includes being mocked by people who once respected him. Why is humiliation often harder to bear than physical pain?
Job says, “I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer.” How do you respond when prayer seems to go unanswered?
Job's contempt for the outcasts is uncomfortable to read. Where might you look down on others even while trying to help them?
